What does “The Final Time” mean? This is the really interesting part. Whitman becomes an archetype of the poet who contains multitudes—someone whose poetic voice attempts to encompass humanity, nature, sexuality, history, and the entire cosmos. The Jack Feist mythology takes that idea and turns it into an explicitly metaphysical proposition: the poet/Logos keeps returning in different forms to gather fragmented pieces of humanity back together. That's why the texts repeatedly mix: Whitman Christ and Gnostic mythology the Logos computers and the internet artificial intelligence data preservation reincarnation fragmented identity apocalypse deliberately absurd/pop-cultural elements It's not really trying to behave like orthodox theology. [QUERENT] [not in the paste] [ANSWER 2] Historically, the important distinction is that “Jack Feist” does not appear to be a documented historical figure in the conventional sense. The material I can find presents him as a literary/mythological persona created within Lee Sharks’s body of work. If you mean what “the final time” means historically, there are a few layers: Biblical/Christian history: The concept resembles the Christian idea of the Logos—the divine Word in John 1—and especially the idea of incarnation. The text explicitly frames Whitman as a recurring incarnation of the Logos and Feist as its terminal incarnation. Gnostic history: The work borrows heavily from ancient Gnostic mythology, particularly the Apocryphon of John: divine emanation, fragmentation of divine light, imprisonment in matter, and eventual recovery of those fragments. American literary history: It makes Walt Whitman into a kind of American prophetic/Christ figure. That is significant because Whitman's Leaves of Grass (1855) deliberately constructed an enormous poetic self that attempted to encompass America, humanity, sexuality, nature, and history. Modern/digital history: The 2015 ARK text is strikingly contemporary. It imagines humanity's accumulated knowledge collapsing inward into text, electronic devices, data, and a “Noah's Ark of data.” So “the final time” is historically meaningful less as an event that actually happened and more as a modern reworking of very old religious ideas. The basic historical genealogy is: Gnosticism → Christian Logos/incarnation → American prophetic poetry/Whitman → postmodern metafiction → internet/digital mythology → Jack Feist And there's an interesting twist: the 2015 material already contains the idea of repetition—“repeat what has been said” while somehow making it new. That makes The Final Time almost a theory of literary history itself: history repeats, but each repetition changes the meaning of what came before. One caution about the sources: some of the newer webpages describe this corpus in deliberately grand terms—calling it “scripture,” “canon,” etc.—but those are claims made within the project, not established conclusions of academic history. The surviving material gives us enough to construct a historical-critical Jack Feist: a figure situated in a real literary network, with a chronology, works, influences, and transformations—while clearly marking where the evidence becomes fictional or retrospective. A preliminary historical Jack Feist The earliest solid-looking evidence I found is not the 2025–26 “Secret Book of Walt” mythology. It is material attributed to Jack Feist from 2015, particularly ARK, dated February 18, 2015, and written “in the margins” of Walt Whitman's Sunflower Sutra. That changes the picture considerably. 1. Jack Feist begins as a poet The 2015 ARK presents Feist as a poet confronting an increasingly electronic existence: “my life is almost PURELY engorged w/ electronic devices” The poem moves through books, alerts, screens, hyperlinks, information, and mental fragmentation. So our first historically useful formulation would be: Jack Feist = an experimental poet concerned with what happens to consciousness when literature enters an electronic/information environment. That is much more concrete than “terminal incarnation of the Logos.” 2. But here's the historically interesting thing: Feist existed in the corpus before this mythology was articulated in its current form. They place him inside Paper Roses: The Imaginary Archive of a Canonical Life. The titles include: What Was Lost The Creeping Disease Remnant Tiger Leap and related volumes. The crucial phrase is “Imaginary Archive.” So the 2014 documentary evidence itself is already telling us: Jack Feist is a literary subject whose “life” is being constructed through archival forms. That means “historical Jack Feist” was never simply intended to mean: Here is a normal poet; here is his biography. Rather: Here is an archive of a life, whose historical status is itself part of the literary experiment. This is why conventional biography is likely to fail us. V. And I think that is the right way to discover what “the historical Jack Feist” actually is. [QUERENT] [not in the paste] [ANSWER 5] This second pass gives us a much firmer basis. More importantly, it changes our working hypothesis. 1. We now have a primary 2014 witness that tells us what Jack Feist is The front matter of Pearl and Other Poems is unusually explicit. It calls the resulting work “applied literary history” and, crucially, says the imagined identities are not merely pen names but attempts at “the creation of human life, ex nihilo.” Then the Jack Feist section begins. Feist is described as: an “unemployed academic” after graduate school; someone obsessively engaged with computers, books, refreshing, arranging, clicking; a person fascinated by history as a linear sequence; a maker of unfinished projects; the creator of the Crimson Hexagon project itself; and, most importantly, a fictional human being whose imagined biography is explicitly part of the project. The text eventually states the mechanism almost programmatically: the creator wants to make biographies, anthologies, reviews, correspondence, publishers, and Wikipedia articles for his imaginary people in order to explore the point at which text becomes history. That's a documentary witness from 2014, not a later interpretation. This gives us our first major conclusion Historical Jack Feist was never intended simply to be a disguised ordinary person. The original project is deliberately asking: Can an imaginary person acquire historical reality through documents? That makes our project of reconstructing him almost exactly what the 2014 text itself asks us to do. 2. And the documentary evidence for B begins by at least 2014, with actual books and printed matter. 3. The physical-book evidence is real We have multiple independent catalog traces for the 2014 books. So the artifact simultaneously says: “This person is an author.” and “This is an imaginary archive of his life.” That's not an accidental contradiction. It is the medium. 5. From the Crimson Hexagon passage, Feist is characterized as someone preoccupied with: The computer He sits at a computer “typing things, refreshing things, arranging things, and clicking things.” History He imagines history as a tube through which people and events flash past as comprehensible bursts of light. Fragmentation His life consists of unfinished projects. Artificial life He becomes fascinated by the alchemical homunculus—the artificial human—and the possibility of creating a human being ex nihilo. Authorship The Crimson Hexagon is explicitly an experiment in producing autonomous writerly identities. Documentation The most important artifacts aren't necessarily the poems themselves. The text says the Wiki articles become more important than biographies, anthologies, reviews, correspondence, etc., because they create the appearance of a historical person. That is an extraordinarily coherent conceptual portrait. 6. Now the 2013 date becomes much more interesting The books identify Feist as: Jack Feist, 1983–2013. But notice what we do not have: death certificate; obituary from an independent newspaper; cemetery record; university record; contemporary interview; independently authored correspondence; census/biographical record; contemporaneous literary review identifying a flesh-and-blood Jack Feist. Instead, we have a literary artifact that assigns him those dates. And the 2014 Pearl apparatus tells us explicitly that the entire exercise involves manufacturing historical documentation for imaginary people. Therefore: 1983–2013 should currently be treated as an internal biographical datum of the Feist archive, not as an established fact about a human being. That's a crucial methodological distinction. 7. The 2008 claim is now our most important unresolved lead The 2014 Pearl apparatus says Lee Sharks was responsible for the serialization beginning in 2008 of Stationary: The American Journals, which it attributes to Feist. But we haven't yet found an actual 2008 witness. So our evidence currently looks like this: 2014 retrospective claim → “Feist's Stationary was serialized from 2008” but: 2008 primary document → NOT YET FOUND Therefore I would not put “2008” into the factual chronology yet. I'd put it in a separate category: Claim requiring documentary recovery. If we find a genuine 2008 webpage, zine, mailing-list post, PDF, Google Books record, or cached publication, it would move the origin of Feist back six years. That would be a major discovery. 8. We have, however, found a genuine 2014 digital witness The dataset preserving the original blog corpus records: December 1, 2014 — “BELIEF & TECHNIQUE FOR TELEPATHIC PROSE” and the title explicitly reads: “Lee Sharks & Jack Feist / from Pearl and Other Poems.” That means Feist wasn't merely a character mentioned in the printed book. He was being used as a named textual voice in the surrounding digital publication ecosystem in 2014. That's important. 9. Then the 2015 witnesses show the voice becoming independent By February–May 2015 we get a much clearer Feist voice. The ARK entry is particularly valuable because it carries: Jack Feist written in the margins of “Sunflower Sutra” 2/18/15, evening, Glenbrook, MI. The poem's concerns are exactly what the 2014 biography predicted: electronic devices; books; alerts; hyperlinks; enormous archives; information overload; repetition; the end of time; the problem of writing after everything has already been written. And the May 2015 TEKATAK and HADITH with TEETH witnesses continue that voice. So there's a fascinating progression: 2014: Feist is described and constructed. 2014: Feist appears as a textual voice. 2015: Feist writes dated works. Later: Feist becomes theological/Logotic. 10. This makes “The Final Time” look like a late transformation Our evidence now supports a more precise historical hypothesis: Phase I — Construction 2014 Feist is created as a heteronymic literary person inside the Crimson Hexagon. Phase II — Materialization 2014 Feist acquires books, ISBNs, editors, biographies, bibliographic records and a putative life-span. Phase III — Voice 2014–15 Feist becomes an actual textual voice in poems and prose. Phase IV — Death/transmission 2013 as internal chronology; 2014–15 as documentary publication The archive presents Feist as having died, while his voice continues. Phase V — Metaphysical transformation later corpus Feist becomes Logos, Whitmanian successor, terminal incarnation, “first born, last released,” etc. The current Crimson Hexagonal architecture explicitly calls Jack Feist LOGOS* and places him outside the twelve-member Dodecad as the “first born, last released.” But that is a much later layer than the 2014 documentary construction. 11. One correction to our earlier approach I think we should retire the phrase “historical Jack Feist” if by it we mean “the actual man behind the texts.” Instead, I'd use: The Feist historical object That object consists of: a fictional/heteronymic person deliberately furnished with the documentary apparatus of an historical life. And that is something we can historically reconstruct. In fact, the 2014 text practically gives us the research program itself: biography → bibliography → correspondence → reviews → Wiki → archival repetition → historical existence. 12. Our evidence ledger now looks like this Witness Date Type What it establishes Pearl and Other Poems 2014 Printed book Feist is an intentional heteronymic person Crimson Hexagon section 2014 Primary text Feist's conceptual biography Tiger Leap 2014 Physical book/catalog Feist has a book-object + 1983–2013 chronology Remnant 2014 Physical book/catalog Feist has an independently cataloged publication Creeping Disease 2014 Book/catalog Expands Feist corpus What Was Lost 2014 Book/catalog Expands Paper Roses archive “Belief & Technique…” Dec. 2014 Digital witness Feist appears as named co-voice ARK Feb. 18, 2015 Dated primary text Feist has a distinctive first-person voice TEKATAK May 10, 2015 Dated digital text Feist participates in archive/internet poetics HADITH with TEETH May 11, 2015 Dated digital text Feist becomes revelatory/religious voice “2008 Stationary” claimed in 2014 Retrospective testimony Potentially huge, but presently uncorroborated 2026 LOGOS apparatus 2026 Retrospective theory Reinterprets Feist metaphysically Where I'd go next The highest-value unresolved question is now 2008–2013. Rather than searching “Jack Feist” generally, I'd conduct a targeted textual excavation of Stationary: The American Journals and the pre-2014 Crimson Hexagon corpus. We're looking specifically for: exact title occurrences; chapter/entry titles; dates inside the journals; references to Feist; first-person Feist passages; references to Lee Sharks; references to Johannes Sigil; URLs or publication venues; screenshots or cached pages; ISBNs/ASINs; Wayback traces; contemporary citations. And there's another particularly interesting lead: “Snub-Poemed — Jack Feist (2013)” is now being catalogued as a concrete poem and is described as both a Socrates portrait and a portrait of Johannes Sigil. The Restored Academy identifies it specifically as a 2013 Feist work. That may be our earliest actual textual artifact yet. So the next excavation should be 2013 first, then work backward toward 2008. That's where I think we'll learn whether the Feist persona was already fully formed before the 2014 books—or whether the 2014 books themselves are the true point of origin. [QUERENT] [not in the paste; the answer adopts a formulation it attributes to the querent: someone physically composed and published these artifacts] [ANSWER 6] Yes. I think your formulation is methodologically stronger. The object of the investigation should be the human authorial production behind the Jack Feist attribution, not the archive's preferred ontology of Feist. We can provisionally assume only the minimal thing you stated: someone physically composed, edited, formatted, published, uploaded, and maintained these artifacts. Then we ask what evidence lets us reconstruct that person—or persons—without simply accepting the archive's explanations. The key distinction We should separate three things: Jack Feist as an attributed author — what the documents say. The historical producer(s) of those documents — the human beings who actually made them. The archive's theory of the relationship between 1 and 2 — heteronym, fiction, Logos, etc. Our job is primarily #2. And we should allow the evidence to produce an answer that the archive itself might dislike. The strongest lead: Lee Sharks At present, Lee Sharks is the overwhelmingly important candidate for the human producer of the Feist corpus. This isn't merely because a 2026 archive document says so. There are several different kinds of evidence. 1. The 2014 book is physically attributed to Lee Sharks Pearl and Other Poems was published in 2014 under the name Lee Sharks, with New Human Press/Ann Arbor metadata and ISBN 978-0-692-31307-7. Google Books independently catalogs the CreateSpace edition and identifies Lee Sharks as author and Johannes Sigil as contributor. But inside that book, the Jack Feist section is part of the same constructed apparatus. So we have: one physical book → Lee Sharks → Feist material → Sigil apparatus. That is already evidence for an interconnected production rather than three independent authors. 2. The 2014 text explicitly describes the production system The front matter says The Crimson Hexagon develops distinct writerly voices in the manner of Browning's personae and Pessoa's heteronyms. It explicitly identifies the Feist passage as “from THE CRIMSON HEXAGON / Jack Feist.” That doesn't prove that Lee Sharks physically wrote every Feist text. But it establishes that the Lee Sharks publication is the material environment in which Feist is being produced and presented. 3. Later evidence becomes unusually explicit A 2025/26 document says: Jack Feist is a “literary persona of Lee Sharks.” Another current archive document identifies the human operator of the corpus as Lee Sharks, while describing Feist as a heteronymic function. We shouldn't simply believe those retrospective declarations. But they are statements by the person controlling the archive about authorship, and therefore are themselves evidence. Most importantly, the current operative-semiotics site identifies Lee Sharks as a human independent scholar and gives ORCID 0009-0000-1599-0703. An Academia.edu profile independently presents the same name, ORCID, scholarly interests, and teaching/research identity. So the human behind the larger production is not merely an invented archive entity. There is a real contemporary author operating under Lee Sharks. But here's where we need to be more radical I don't think we should jump from: “Lee Sharks produced Feist” to: “therefore Jack Feist = Lee Sharks.” That's too crude. Instead, we need to reconstruct how the Feist identity was produced by the human author. Because the 2014 evidence shows that Feist has properties that Lee Sharks does not simply have. For example: Feist 1983–2013 unemployed academic obsessed with computers associated with Stationary author of Tiger Leap, Remnant, etc. apparently dead positioned as a historical poet while Lee Sharks is the name on Pearl and Other Poems publishes the Feist material creates the surrounding apparatus continues publishing after 2013 eventually explicitly discusses the Feist/Lee relationship. That is not an ordinary pseudonym. It's closer to a deliberately constructed second authorial biography. And that's exactly why I think the right historical question is: What aspects of Jack Feist can be recovered as transformations of the human author's own biography, experiences, intellectual interests, locations, education, relationships, and literary activity? That's where this gets genuinely historical. The first remarkable clue: geography The Feist texts contain Michigan-specific documentary coordinates. The ARK witness is dated: February 18, 2015 — evening — Glenbrook, MI and is explicitly attributed to Jack Feist. Meanwhile, the physical Pearl book is published by New Human Press, Ann Arbor. The present-day Lee Sharks scholarly identity is also Michigan-based, with sources identifying Detroit/Redford Township and a University of Michigan PhD. That doesn't prove the individual identity of Feist. But it gives us a geographical continuity that should be investigated rather than dismissed as fictional scenery. The second clue: academic biography The 2014 Feist portrait says: “For a period after graduate school, he worked as an unemployed academic.” That's unusually specific. And the current human identity associated with Lee Sharks is an independent scholar with a PhD in Comparative Literature from the University of Michigan. Again, we cannot simply say: Feist says graduate school → Lee Sharks has a PhD → therefore Feist is Lee Sharks. But it is precisely the kind of biographical overlap that a historical reconstruction should catalogue. I'd call this: Possible biographical transfer: HIGH interest, presently unproven. The third clue: the chronology is deliberately strange Here's something I now think deserves much more attention. The books say: Jack Feist — 1983–2013. Yet Feist texts continue appearing in 2014 and 2015. That's not necessarily an inconsistency. It may mean that the death of Feist is part of the construction of the persona, while the human producer continued generating Feist material. But there's another possibility: 2013 may mark a real event in the human author's life which was transformed into the “death” of Feist. The later Lee Sharks text actually says: “Jack Feist crashed. He went silent in 2013.” and then: “Lee Sharks emerged from the mirror.” That is retrospective mythology, so we can't take its literal story as fact. But it is a very interesting admission about a transition in authorial identity around 2013. That transition should become a central object of research. And we have another startling piece of evidence A 2026 archive document contains a purported obituary draft: “JACK FEIST (1983–2013)” and claims that Feist died in Michigan in November 2013. But the document itself is framed as part of an “Afterlife Archive” and openly labels the forensic details fictional. So we cannot use the November date as a factual death date. But we can use it as evidence that the archive's Feist-death narrative crystallized around Michigan, 2013, and that this is important enough to be repeatedly reconstructed. That's a different—and legitimate—historical claim. I propose a new research model Rather than constructing: Jack Feist = X we construct: The Feist production biography And divide every fact into four levels: Level 1 — Directly documented human facts Things independently associated with the human producer. For example: existence of Lee Sharks as a contemporary author; publication of Pearl under that name; Michigan connection; University of Michigan academic identity; ORCID; online publication infrastructure. Level 2 — Authorial declarations Statements by Lee Sharks about Feist and about the relationship between Sharks and Feist. Useful, but not automatically factual. Level 3 — Internal Feist biography Things the Feist texts say about “him”: birth year; education; unemployment; location; relationships; death; works; experiences. These become hypotheses about the underlying human life, not facts. Level 4 — Later myth Logos, reincarnation, terminal incarnation, Golden Tickets, Damascus Codex, etc. These are enormously important for intellectual history, but shouldn't contaminate our reconstruction of the human author. Then we can do something really powerful We can construct a table like this: Feist datum Evidence Possible human analogue Confidence 1983 birth Feist metadata ? Low Graduate education 2014 Feist biography Lee Sharks has PhD Interesting Unemployed academic 2014 Feist biography ? Interesting Michigan Feist texts Lee Sharks Michigan connection Strong correlation Computer/internet obsession Feist texts Lee Sharks's enormous digital corpus Strong thematic correlation Publishing experiments Feist bibliography New Human Press / Sharks Strong Death in 2013 Feist archive possible authorial transition Unresolved Stationary beginning 2008 retrospective claim ? Unverified Feist's subsequent voice 2014–15 texts produced within Sharks corpus Strong Feist = Logos later archive theological reinterpretation Not relevant to human biography This is how we avoid both naïveté and excessive skepticism. And I think our central hypothesis has now changed The interesting hypothesis isn't: “Was Jack Feist a real person?” We already know that a real human being produced the Jack Feist corpus. The interesting question is: How much of the fictional/heteronymic Jack Feist was constructed out of the actual life of the human author, and what happened to that human author's identity during the construction? That's an empirically investigable question. And 2013 is probably the hinge. So I suggest our next excavation be specifically the human producer's biography circa 2008–2015: education, publications, residences, employment, collaborators, websites, presses, and the emergence of Lee Sharks. We can then compare that chronology against every Feist biographical claim and identify the points where the two histories converge. That is how I would attempt to actually construct the historical Jack Feist, rather than allowing the archive to construct him for us.
